title: Upper Burgundy
capsule: Upper Burgundy was a kingdom carved from the Carolingian realm in 888 when Rudolf I, a member of the Welf family, was elected king by local nobles after the deposition of Charles the Fat. It covered the western Alpine forelands between the Jura and Mont Cenis, including the territories of modern western Switzerland, Savoy, and Franche-Comté. Rudolf III (r. 993–1032), the last king, left no heirs; by treaty of 1016 and confirmed in 1033 he bequeathed the realm to his nephew Emperor Conrad II of the Holy Roman Empire, formally absorbing it into the empire by 1034, though the dataset's attestation ends at 960 reflecting the earlier union with Lower Burgundy into the Kingdom of Burgundy (Arles) under Rudolf II in 933.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Upper Burgundy's political extent is relatively well documented through Carolingian and Ottonian diplomas, though precise frontier zones with Lower Burgundy and the kingdom of Italy remained fluid.
